{{Short description|Family of logics for natural-language and counterfactual conditionals}}
{{About|the family of logics for ''if''-sentences|the truth-functional connective|Material conditional}}
{{AI-generated|date=December 2025}}

'''Conditional logic''' (also: '''the logic of conditionals''') refers to a family of formal systems for reasoning with statements of the form "if ''A'', (then) ''B''". Conditional logics are intended to capture the meaning and patterns of inference associated with natural language conditionals more faithfully than the classical [[material conditional]], which gives rise to well-known paradoxes.<ref name="Edgington2020">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Edgington |first=Dorothy |title=Indicative Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |date=2020 |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/conditionals/}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Conditional logics are used in [[philosophical logic]], [[Formal semantics (natural language)|formal semantics of natural language]], [[artificial intelligence]], and the [[psychology of reasoning]]. They are used to model everyday and scientific reasoning about hypothetical, causal, modal, and counterfactual scenarios.<ref name="Starr2019">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Starr|first=William B.|title=Counterfactuals|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|date=2019|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/counterfactuals/|quote=In the philosophical literature, one also sees a different notation due to David Lewis (1973b,c): A □→ C. (Lewis also uses A ⬦→ C for ''might''-counterfactuals.) These notations are about as prevalent in the literature.}}</ref><ref name="Adams1975" />

The material conditional is a truth function, which is always true except when the antecedent is true and the consequent false. Most conditional logics introduce an additional conditional connective (often written <math>\mathbin{>}</math> or, in the context of [[Counterfactual conditional|counterfactuals]], <math>\square\to</math>) whose truth or acceptability can depend on similarity between possible worlds, on context and background information, or on probabilistic support rather than on a simple two-valued truth table.<ref name="Stalnaker1968" /><ref name="Lewis1973" /> These systems are designed to validate basic principles such as [[modus ponens]], while restricting or invalidating classical schemas like strengthening the antecedent, transitivity, and contraposition, which are not always correct for ordinary "if ... then ..." sentences.<ref name="Edgington2020" /><ref name=":0" /> It is common to distinguish between  [[indicative conditional]]s, which concern open possibilities relative to what is currently known, and [[counterfactual conditional]]s, which describe ways things would or might have been contrary to fact. However, many conditional logics treat both of these as variants of a common underlying framework.<ref name="Edgington2020" /><ref name="Starr2019" />

A wide range of semantic approaches has been developed for such logics, including three-valued and other many-valued systems that treat conditionals with false antecedents as void, [[Possible worlds semantics|possible worlds]] and selection function models in the tradition of Stalnaker and Lewis, premise or ordering source semantics, probabilistic and suppositional accounts tying acceptability to conditional probability, and belief revision frameworks based on the [[Ramsey test]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Adams1975" /> Corresponding proof-theoretic systems range from Chellas's basic logics '''Ck''' and '''CK''' to stronger systems such as Burgess's '''B''' and Lewis's '''V''', '''VW''' and '''VC''', or Stalnaker's '''C2''', which validate different structural principles for the conditional connective and are often related by soundness and completeness theorems to the underlying semantic frameworks.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="StalnakerThomason1970" /><ref name="Lewis1973" /> Conditional logics are also closely linked to nonmonotonic consequence relations and default reasoning systems, notably the cumulative and preferential systems '''C''' and '''P''' of Kraus, Lehmann and Magidor, which are widely used in AI to formalize rules with exceptions.<ref name="KLM1990" />

Historically, conditional logic grew out of attempts to refine earlier notions such as C. I. Lewis's [[strict conditional|strict implication]], and the contemporary field is usually traced to Robert Stalnaker's 1968 possible worlds theory of conditionals and David Lewis's subsequent development of variably strict logics for counterfactuals.<ref name="Stalnaker1968" /><ref name="Lewis1973" /> Later work by Nute, Burgess, Kratzer, Gärdenfors and many others has broadened the landscape, yielding a cluster of interrelated frameworks rather than a single canonical system and connecting the logic of "if ... then ..." with topics such as [[nonmonotonic logic]], [[belief revision]], [[conditional probability]] and the pragmatics of assertion, questioning and decision-making.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Gärdenfors1988" />

==Overview==
Conditional logics form a family of formal systems for reasoning with sentences of the form "if ''A'', (then) ''B''". They aim to explain when such conditionals are acceptable, how they interact with other logical operators, and which arguments involving them should count as valid or rationally compelling. In contrast to the classical material conditional <math>A \supset B</math>, most conditional logics build some notion of dependence between antecedent and consequent into their semantics, and allow the validity of inferences with conditionals to be sensitive to context, background information, or normality assumptions.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Edgington2020" />

Rather than a single canonical calculus, ''conditional logic'' is now used as an umbrella term for several families of interrelated systems. Prominent traditions include: three-valued and other many-valued logics that treat conditionals with false antecedents as void; possible worlds and selection function logics inspired by Stalnaker and Lewis; premise or ordering source semantics that work with sets of background assumptions; probabilistic and suppositional accounts that tie acceptability to conditional probability; and belief revision and nonmonotonic approaches grounded in the [[Ramsey test]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Stalnaker1968" /><ref name="Lewis1973" /><ref name="Adams1975">{{cite book |last=Adams |first=Ernest W. |year=1975 |title=The Logic of Conditionals |publisher=Reidel}}</ref><ref name="Gärdenfors1988"/> A common slogan is that to evaluate "if ''A'', then ''B''" one should ''add'' ''A'' hypothetically to one's information state and ask whether ''B'' would then be accepted.

Most authors distinguish between [[indicative conditional]]s, which concern open possibilities relative to an information state, and [[counterfactual conditional]]s, which describe ways things ''would'' or ''might'' have been contrary to fact (for example, "If the match had been struck, it would have lit"). Many formal frameworks nevertheless treat these as variants of a common semantic core, parametrized by the kind of [[Modality (semantics)#Force and flavor|modality]] or background premises involved.<ref name="Edgington2020" /><ref name="Starr2019" /><ref name=":0" /> This article follows that practice and surveys a range of systems that have been proposed for both indicative and counterfactual readings.

=== Notation ===
The conditional studied by a given conditional logic is here notated with <math>\mathbin{>}</math>, for instance <math>A \mathbin{>} B</math> represents "if A, then B". This conditional "corner", not to be confused with the indentically written [[greater than sign]], was the notation used by [[Robert Stalnaker]]'s paper that started the field (see {{section link||History}} below),<ref name="Stalnaker1968" /> and which has been followed in various other reference publications.<ref>{{Citation|chapter=Conditional Logic|chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-6259-0_8|publisher=Springer Netherlands|title=Handbook of Philosophical Logic: Volume II: Extensions of Classical Logic|date=1984|access-date=2025-12-02|place=Dordrecht|isbn=978-94-009-6259-0|pages=387–439|doi=10.1007/978-94-009-6259-0_8|language=en|first=Donald|last=Nute|editor-first=D.|editor-last=Gabbay|editor2-first=F.|editor2-last=Guenthner}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Some conditional logics have been studied in the specific context of [[counterfactual conditional]]s, and in that context, [[David Lewis (philosopher)|David Lewis]]'s <math>A \; \square\to B</math> notation for counterfactuals (read "if A had been the case, B would have been the case") is also common.<ref name="Starr2019" />

=== Interaction with modality and speech acts ===
{{Main|Indicative conditional|Counterfactual conditional}}

In many languages, ''if''-clauses interact closely with overt or covert modal expressions such as ''must'', ''might'', or ''would''. On the influential "restrictor" view, an ''if''-clause does not itself introduce a binary connective, but instead restricts the domain of a following modal or quantificational operator; this helps explain the apparent commutation of conditionals and modals in sentences like "if ''A'', it must be that ''B''" and "it must be that if ''A'', then ''B''".<ref>{{cite book |last=Kratzer |first=Angelika |year=2012 |title=Modals and Conditionals |publisher=OUP}}</ref>

Dynamic and expressivist accounts build on this idea by treating an indicative or counterfactual conditional as an update on an information state or conversational scoreboard. On such views, incompatibilities between "if ''A'', ''B''" and "if ''A'', might not ''B''" arise because the two updates place conflicting constraints on the same body of shared information. The same machinery extends naturally to conditional questions (''if A, will B?'') and to conditional imperatives (''if A, do B''), which are modelled as transformations of inquiry states or decision problems rather than as simple truth evaluations.<ref>{{cite journal |last=von Fintel |first=Kai |year=2001 |title=Counterfactuals in a Dynamic Context |journal=In Ken Hale: A Life in Language}}</ref><ref name="Starr2019" />

In this way, conditional logics are used not only to model the truth conditions of ''if''-sentences, but also to capture their role in conversation, planning and decision, and to connect the semantics of conditionals with the pragmatics of assertion, questioning and commanding.<ref name=":0" />

=== Logical principles and their failure ===

Classical material implication validates a number of principles that look plausible at first sight but seem problematic for ordinary ''if''-sentences. Early work by Adams, Stalnaker and Lewis highlighted counterexamples to strengthening the antecedent (from "if ''A'' then ''C''" infer "if ''A'' and ''B'' then ''C''"), to transitivity (chaining conditionals), and to contraposition (from "if ''A'' then ''B''" infer "if not ''B'' then not ''A''").<ref name="Stalnaker1968" /><ref name="Lewis1973" /><ref name="Edgington2020" /><ref name="Starr2019" />

Modern conditional logics typically invalidate at least some of these principles. They also differ with respect to more specific schemas such as:
* '''Or-to-If''' (from <math>A \lor B</math> infer <math>\neg A \mathbin{>} B</math>);
* '''Import–export''' (<math>A \mathbin{>} (B \mathbin{>} C)</math> equivalent to <math>(A \land B) \mathbin{>} C</math>);
* '''Simplification of disjunctive antecedents''' (from <math>(A \lor B) \mathbin{>} C</math> infer both <math>A \mathbin{>} C</math> and <math>B \mathbin{>} C</math>).

The status of these schemata is tied to fine-grained issues about how similarity orderings or selection functions work, how contexts are updated, and how conditionals interact with background premises. For example, variably strict semantics that evaluate conditionals at "closest" antecedent worlds tend to be nonmonotonic on the left: adding extra conditions to the antecedent can shift attention to more remote worlds and thereby defeat an inference.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Starr2019" /> Questions about which schemas to adopt are central to the classification of conditional logics, and help motivate the array of systems ('''CK''', '''B''', '''V''', '''VC''', '''C2''' and others) discussed in later sections.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Chellas1975">{{cite journal |last=Chellas |first=Brian F. |year=1975 |title=Basic Conditional Logic |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=133–153 |doi=10.1007/BF00693270 }}</ref>

=== Relation to nonmonotonic reasoning and AI ===

Conditional logics are closely connected to nonmonotonic logics and to AI formalisms for default and defeasible reasoning. Preferential and ranked models for nonmonotonic consequence relations, introduced by Kraus, Lehmann and Magidor, can be understood as abstracting away from the explicit conditional connective and instead working directly with a consequence relation <math>\vdash_{\!\sim}</math> that encodes defaults of the form "normally, if ''A'' then ''B''". Their system '''P''' of preferential entailment, and the stronger rational system '''R''', correspond to the "flat" fragments of several variably strict conditional logics, including Burgess's system '''B''' and Lewis's systems for counterfactuals.<ref name="KLM1990" /><ref name=":0" />

From the perspective of artificial intelligence, these logics support representation and automated reasoning with rules that have exceptions: for example, that birds normally fly, or that a component normally functions unless it is known to be faulty. The correspondence between conditional logics and nonmonotonic consequence relations has been used to transfer results and techniques between the two areas, to design theorem provers for conditional logics, and to apply them in diagnosis, planning and knowledge representation.<ref name="KLM1990" /><ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Horty |first=John F. |title=Logic and Artificial Intelligence |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |edition=Winter 2021 |year=2018 |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2021/entries/logic-ai/}}</ref><ref name="Olivetti 2007 22">{{cite journal |last=Olivetti |first=Nicola |author2=Pozzato, Gian Luca |author3=Schwind, Camilla B. |year=2007 |title=A Sequent Calculus and a Theorem Prover for Standard Conditional Logics |journal=ACM Transactions on Computational Logic |volume=8 |issue=4 |page=22 |doi=10.1145/1276920.1276924 }}</ref>

== History ==
Early modern logic identified "if ''A'' then ''B''" with the material implication true in all cases except when ''A'' is true and ''B'' false. While attractive for mathematical proof, this leads to the [[paradoxes of material implication]] (any true ''B'' or false ''A'' makes ''A ⊃ B'' true) and counterintuitive behavior of negation and denial. Classical analyses also vacuously validate counterfactuals with false antecedents.<ref>{{cite book |last=Whitehead |first=Alfred N. |author2=Russell, Bertrand |title=Principia Mathematica |year=1910 |publisher=CUP}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Quine |first=W. V. O. |title=Methods of Logic |year=1950 |publisher=Holt}}</ref> These issues motivated richer accounts distinguishing [[indicative conditional]]s from [[counterfactual conditional]]s and modeling the dependency between antecedent and consequent.

Although systems for reasoning with conditionals go back at least to [[C. I. Lewis]]'s strict implication and related modal logics, the contemporary field of '''conditional logic''' is usually traced to [[Robert Stalnaker]]'s 1968 paper ''A Theory of Conditionals''.<ref name="Stalnaker1968" /> Drawing on [[Frank P. Ramsey|Ramsey]]'s idea of hypothetically adding the antecedent to one's belief state (the [[Ramsey test]]), Stalnaker proposed a [[possible worlds semantics]] in which an indicative or counterfactual conditional is true just in case its consequent holds at the "closest" antecedent worlds. This provided a unified account of ordinary and counterfactual conditionals, explained the failure of principles such as Transitivity and Strengthening the Antecedent, and suggested a corresponding modal logic of a non-material conditional connective.

[[File:Lewis's logics of counterfactuals.svg|thumb|[[David Lewis (philosopher)|David Lewis]]'s logics of counterfactuals]]
Stalnaker's framework was soon generalized and made more systematic. In a joint paper, Stalnaker and [[Richmond Thomason]] gave a fully explicit semantics and axiomatization for conditional logics in terms of selection functions that pick, for each world and antecedent proposition, a set of closest antecedent worlds, thereby turning Stalnaker's informal proposal into a family of well-behaved formal systems.<ref name="StalnakerThomason1970">{{cite journal |last1=Stalnaker |first1=Robert C. |last2=Thomason |first2=Richmond H. |year=1970 |title=A Semantic Analysis of Conditional Logic |journal=Theoria |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=23–42 |doi=10.1111/j.1755-2567.1970.tb00408.x}}</ref> Around the same time, David Lewis developed an alternative but closely related "variably strict" account using comparative similarity orderings over possible worlds, culminating in his monograph ''Counterfactuals'' and a hierarchy of systems (V, VW, VC) for counterfactual conditionals.<ref name="Lewis1973" /> These works established the now standard picture of conditionals evaluated relative to similarity or selection among possible worlds, and they framed many of the central questions about which structural principles such logics should validate.

During the mid-1970s and early 1980s, researchers working in the Stalnaker–Lewis tradition developed a shared axiomatic and semantic toolkit. Brian Chellas introduced the system '''CK''' (and its hyperintensional variant '''Ck''') as a "basic conditional logic", corresponding to the core selection function semantics and serving as an analogue of the normal modal logic K for conditionals.<ref name="Chellas1975"/> John Burgess later supplied simplified completeness proofs for a range of conditional logics and introduced system '''B''', tied to ordering semantics.<ref name="Burgess1981"/> Donald Nute's monograph ''Topics in Conditional Logic'' (1980) synthesized these developments, systematizing selection function, ordering, and relative modality frameworks and mapping out the space of normal conditional logics that extend CK in different ways.<ref name="Nute1980"/>

By the late 1980s and 1990s, conditional logic had become tightly connected with work on nonmonotonic reasoning and probabilistic conditionals. Ernest W. Adams had already proposed a high probability consequence relation for simple indicative conditionals, based on identifying the acceptability of "if ''A'' then ''B''" with a high conditional probability ''P(B|A)''.<ref name="Adams1975"/> Building on both the [[Counterfactual conditional#Variably strict conditional|Stalnaker–Lewis semantics]] and Adams's ideas, Kraus, Lehmann, and Magidor introduced preferential and cumulative models for defeasible conditionals, and defined the nonmonotonic consequence system '''P''', which can be seen as corresponding to the "flat" (non-nested) fragment of several variably strict conditional logics and of Burgess's system '''B'''.<ref name="Kraus 1990 167–207">{{cite journal |last=Kraus |first=Sarit |author2=Lehmann, Daniel |author3=Magidor, Menachem |year=1990 |title=Nonmonotonic Reasoning, Preferential Models and Cumulative Logics |journal=Artificial Intelligence |volume=44 |issue=1–2 |pages=167–207 |doi=10.1016/0004-3702(90)90101-5 }}</ref> This work cemented the role of conditional logics as a link between philosophical analyses of "if ... then ..." and AI formalisms for default and defeasible inference.

In parallel, possible worlds approaches spawned alternative but equivalent perspectives. Premise based and "ordering source" semantics, originating with Frank Veltman and further developed by Lewis and Angelika Kratzer, reinterpreted conditionals in terms of sets of background premises or ordering sources that are updated or restricted by the antecedent, showing how similarity based models could be recast in more explicitly epistemic and dynamic terms.<ref name="Veltman 1976">{{cite journal |last=Veltman |first=Frank |year=1976 |title=Prejudices, Presuppositions and the Theory of Counterfactuals |journal=Amsterdam Papers in Formal Grammar}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Lewis |first=David |year=1981 |title=Ordering Semantics and Premise Semantics for Counterfactuals |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=217–234 |doi=10.1007/BF00248850 }}</ref><ref name="Kratzer 2012">{{cite book |last=Kratzer |first=Angelika |year=2012 |title=Modals and Conditionals: New and Revised Perspectives |publisher=OUP}}</ref> At the same time, belief revision theorists such as [[Peter Gärdenfors]] investigated conditionals via [[Belief revision|AGM revision]] and the [[Ramsey test]], while proof theorists developed sequent and tableau calculi for many of the main systems of conditional logic.<ref name="Gärdenfors1988"/><ref name="Olivetti 2007 22"/>

More recently, survey articles and handbooks have emphasized that conditional logic is not a single system but a cluster of related frameworks: trivalent, possible worlds, premise based, probabilistic, and belief revision based that can often be intertranslated or shown to share a common "flat" fragment. The ''[[Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]'' entry on the logic of conditionals, for example, situates Stalnaker's 1968 proposal as a central ancestor of modern conditional logics and highlights how later work by Lewis, Nute, Burgess, Kratzer, Kraus–Lehmann–Magidor, and others has diversified and refined the field over the past half century.<ref name=":0">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Égré |first=Paul |author2=Rott, Hans |title=The Logic of Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |edition=Fall 2021 |year=2021 |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2021/entries/logic-conditionals/}}</ref>

== Semantics ==
Conditional logics are often grouped by their semantic framework.

=== Truth-functional and trivalent approaches ===
Some systems remain truth-functional but use more than two truth values. Łukasiewicz introduced a three-valued logic; de Finetti later argued that "if ''A'' then ''B''" should be ''void'' when ''A'' is false (a bet is called off). Modern trivalent systems (e.g., Cooper/Cantwell's and de Finetti–inspired logics) typically validate [[modus ponens]] but invalidate [[modus tollens]] and [[contraposition]]. They aim to block material implication paradoxes and to connect to suppositional/probabilistic intuitions.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Łukasiewicz |first=Jan |year=1920 |title=On Three-Valued Logic |journal=Ruch Filozoficzny}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=de Finetti |first=Bruno |year=1936 |title=La logique de la probabilité |journal=Actes du Congrès International de Philosophie Scientifique}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Égré |first=Paul |author2=Rossi, Lorenzo |author3=Sprenger, Jan |year=2021 |title=De Finettian Logics of Indicative Conditionals: Trivalent Semantics and Validity |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |doi=10.1007/s10992-020-09549-6|hdl=2318/1851003 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Possible worlds semantics ===
A dominant intensional tradition treats conditionals as quantifying over accessible or similar worlds.

* '''Strict conditional''' (C. I. Lewis): <math>A \mathbin{>} B \;\equiv\; \Box(A \supset B)</math>. Powerful, but too strong for natural language (validates strengthening, transitivity, and contraposition).<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lewis |first=C. I. |year=1912 |title=Implication and the Algebra of Logic |journal=Mind |issue=84 |pages=522–531 |doi=10.1093/mind/XXI.84.522 }}</ref>
* '''Variably strict''' (Stalnaker–Lewis): truth depends on the closest ''A''-worlds (given a contextually supplied similarity or selection function). These invalidate strengthening, transitivity, and contraposition, better fitting linguistic data.<ref name="Stalnaker1968">{{cite journal |last=Stalnaker |first=Robert C. |year=1968 |title=A Theory of Conditionals |journal=Studies in Logical Theory |pages=98–112}}</ref><ref name="Lewis1973">{{cite book |last=Lewis|first=David|year=1973|title=Counterfactuals|publisher=Blackwell|pages=118–142}}</ref>

Within this family, axiomatic systems range from basic normal logics ('''CK''') to Burgess's '''B''', Lewis's '''V/VW/VC''', and Stalnaker's '''C2'''. Many retain rules like Right Weakening and Conditional K but reject classical schemas such as Strengthening the Antecedent, Transitivity, and Contraposition.<ref name="Chellas1975"/><ref>{{cite journal |last=Burgess |first=John P. |year=1981 |title=Quick Completeness Proofs for Some Logics of Conditionals |journal=Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic |volume=22 |doi=10.1305/ndjfl/1093883341 }}</ref><ref name="Nute1980"/>

=== Nonmonotonic and preferential models ===
In AI, "if ''A'' then normally ''B''" is modeled by preference orderings over states. Kraus, Lehmann, and Magidor's systems '''C/P/R''' characterize rational, defeasible consequence; the flat (non-nested) fragment of several conditional logics coincides with their '''P''' system.<ref name="Kraus 1990 167–207"/><ref>{{cite journal |last=Lehmann |first=Daniel |author2=Magidor, Menachem |year=1992 |title=What does a conditional knowledge base entail? |journal=Artificial Intelligence |volume=55 |pages=1–60 |doi=10.1016/0004-3702(92)90041-U }}</ref>

=== Premise semantics ===
Premise (or ordering source) semantics evaluates "if ''A'' then ''C''" by keeping a maximal subset of background premises consistent with ''A'' and checking whether ''C'' follows. It captures context sensitivity and is equivalent (via theorems) to similarity based ordering semantics.<ref name="Veltman 1976"/><ref name="Kratzer 2012"/><ref>{{cite journal |last=Lewis |first=David |year=1981 |title=Ordering Semantics and Premise Semantics for Counterfactuals |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=10 |issue=2 |doi=10.1007/BF00248850 }}</ref>

=== Probabilistic approaches ===
Adams proposed that for simple (non-nested) indicatives the probability of "if ''A'' then ''B''" equals the conditional probability <math>P(B\mid A)</math>. His consequence relation (preserving high probability) validates the KLM system '''P''' and rejects strengthening, transitivity, and contraposition.<ref name="Adams1975"/> Lewis's triviality results show that identifying ''all'' conditional probabilities with probabilities of (possibly nested) conditionals collapses to trivial constraints; under Stalnaker semantics the probability of a conditional instead matches ''imaging'' on the antecedent, not Bayesian conditioning.<ref name="Lewis1976">{{cite journal |last=Lewis |first=David |year=1976 |title=Probabilities of Conditionals and Conditional Probabilities |journal=Philosophical Review}}</ref> Subsequent work explores product space models and coherence based previsions for compounds of conditionals.<ref>{{cite journal |last=van Fraassen |first=Bas C. |year=1976 |title=Probabilities of Conditionals |journal=Foundations of Probability Theory, Statistical Inference, and Statistical Theories of Science}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=McGee |first=Vann |year=1989 |title=Conditional Probabilities and Compounds of Conditionals |journal=Philosophical Review |volume=98 |issue=4 |pages=485–541 |doi=10.2307/2185116 |jstor=2185116 }}</ref>

=== Belief revision and the Ramsey test ===
{{Main|Belief revision|Ramsey test}}
On the [[Belief revision#The AGM postulates|AGM]] model of belief revision, "if ''A'' then ''B''" is accepted if and only if, after minimally revising a belief set by ''A'', ''B'' is believed. This can be understood as a formal version of the [[Ramsey test]]. Combined with standard AGM postulates this yields a triviality theorem due to Gärdenfors, prompting proposals to weaken the postulates, restrict compounds, or replace revision with update/imaging.<ref name="Gärdenfors1988"/>

=== Relevance and difference-making ===
Beyond topic relevance in [[relevance logic]], many theorists require that ''A'' make a (probabilistic or doxastic) difference to ''B'' for a conditional to be assertable or valid. This motivates confirmational scores (e.g., ''P(B|A)'' > ''P(B)'') and [[connexive logic]] principles, often at the cost of rules like Right Weakening.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Mares |first=Edwin |title=Relevance Logic |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |date=2020 |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-relevance/}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Douven |first=Igor |year=2016 |title=The Epistemology of Indicative Conditionals |publisher=CUP}}</ref>

==Axiom systems==

Many conditional logics are given by [[Hilbert system|Hilbert–style calculi]] extending classical propositional logic with a distinguished conditional connective <math>\mathbin{>}</math>.  A typical system contains all propositional tautologies in the language with <math>\mathbin{>}</math>, is closed under modus ponens, and is further closed under some combination of structural rules and schematic principles for <math>\mathbin{>}</math>.<ref name=":0" /> This section summarizes some historically central systems and their axiomatizations.

=== Core rules and schematic principles ===

Most normal systems for <math>\mathbin{>}</math> are formulated using the following rules, where <math>\vDash</math> is classical consequence and <math>A,B,C,D</math> are formulas:

:* '''(MP) Modus ponens''': from <math>A</math> and <math>A \to B</math>, infer <math>B</math>.
:* '''(LLE) Left logical equivalence''': from <math>\vDash A \equiv B</math>, infer <math>(A \mathbin{>} C) \equiv (B \mathbin{>} C)</math>.
:* '''(RW) Right weakening''': from <math>\vDash C \to D</math>, infer <math>(A \mathbin{>} C) \to (A \mathbin{>} D)</math>.
:* '''(RCK) Conditional K''': from <math>(C_1 \land \cdots \land C_n) \to D</math>, infer <math>[(A \mathbin{>} C_1)\land\cdots\land(A \mathbin{>} C_n)] \to (A \mathbin{>} D)</math>, for any <math>n \ge 0</math>.

A conditional logic is often called '''normal''' when it contains all propositional tautologies and is closed under (MP), (LLE) and (RCK); (RCK) then entails several further principles such as Logical Truth, Right Weakening and And below.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Nute1980">{{cite book |last=Nute |first=Donald |year=1980 |title=Topics in Conditional Logic |publisher=Reidel}}</ref>

Many systems are most conveniently described in terms of which of the following schematic principles they validate (all schemata are schemata of the form "for all formulas <math>A,B,C</math> ..."):<ref name=":0" />

;'''LT''' (Logical truth)
:<math>A \mathbin{>} \top</math>
;'''ID''' (Identity)
:<math>A \mathbin{>} A</math>
;'''AND'''
:<math>((A \mathbin{>} B)\land(A \mathbin{>} C)) \to (A \mathbin{>}(B \land C))</math>
;'''OR'''
:<math>((A \mathbin{>} C)\land(B \mathbin{>} C)) \to ((A \lor B) \mathbin{>} C)</math>
;'''CCut''' (Cautious transitivity)
:<math>((A \mathbin{>} B)\land((A \land B) \mathbin{>} C)) \to (A \mathbin{>} C)</math>
;'''CMon''' (Cautious monotonicity)
:<math>((A \mathbin{>} B)\land(A \mathbin{>} C)) \to ((A \land B) \mathbin{>} C)</math>
;'''Rec''' (Reciprocity)
:<math>((A \mathbin{>} B)\land(B \mathbin{>} A)) \to ((A \mathbin{>} C) \equiv (B \mathbin{>} C))</math>
;'''RMon''' (Rational monotonicity)
:<math>((A \mathbin{>} B)\land \neg(A \mathbin{>} \neg C)) \to ((A \land C) \mathbin{>} B)</math>
;'''SM''' (Stronger-than-material)
:<math>(A \mathbin{>} B) \to (A \to B)</math>
;'''CS''' (Conjunctive sufficiency)
:<math>(A \land B) \to (A \mathbin{>} B)</math>
;'''CEM''' (Conditional excluded middle)
:<math>(A \mathbin{>} B) \lor (A \mathbin{>} \neg B)</math>

These principles are motivated both by selection–function and ordering–semantics for conditionals, and many can be derived in stronger systems rather than taken as primitive axioms.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Chellas1975"/>

=== Basic normal systems: Ck and CK ===

A convenient starting point is Chellas's basic conditional logics '''Ck''' and '''CK''', which correspond to the core selection function semantics for conditionals.<ref name="Chellas1975" /><ref name=":0" />

* '''Ck''' is the minimal system containing all propositional tautologies and closed under (MP) and (RCK).  It may be viewed as a "hyperintensional" base system: it validates (RCK) but not (LLE).
* '''CK''' adds (LLE) to Ck.  Equivalently, CK is the smallest logic containing all propositional tautologies and closed under (MP), (LLE) and (RCK).  In CK, principles (LT), (RW) and (AND) are theorems, while stronger principles such as (ID), (OR), (CMon), (Rec), (RMon), (SM), (CS) and (CEM) are generally not validated.<ref name=":0" />

CK is often taken as the conditional analogue of the normal modal logic K: it axiomatizes the basic variably strict semantics with arbitrary selection functions or similarity orderings, without extra frame conditions.<ref name=":0" />

=== Burgess's system B and its extensions (V, VW, VC, C2, SS, NP) ===

Building on CK, a family of stronger logics is obtained by adding further schemata.  Égré and Rott highlight nine "salient" systems Ck, CK, B, SS, NP, V, VW, VC and C2, all normal in the above sense.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Burgess1981">{{cite journal |last=Burgess |first=John P. |year=1981 |title=Quick Completeness Proofs for Some Logics of Conditionals |journal=Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=76–84 |doi=10.1305/ndjfl/1093883341 }}</ref>

;'''B'''
: Burgess's system '''B''' is the smallest extension of CK in which (ID), (OR) and (CMon) hold; with (RCK) and (LLE) these also yield (AND), (CCut) and (Rec).  In ordering semantics, B corresponds to models in which each world is equipped with a reflexive and transitive similarity preorder.<ref name="Burgess1981" /><ref name=":0" />

;'''V'''
: Lewis's logic '''V''' adds to B the principle (RMon).  Semantically, this corresponds to strengthening the similarity ordering to a weak order (modular, total-preorder–like) at each evaluation world.<ref name="Lewis1973" /><ref name=":0" />

;'''VW'''
: System '''VW''' further extends V by validating (SM), so that every conditional implies the corresponding material conditional.  This makes VW suitable as a weaker "counterfactual" logic that still preserves modus ponens in the usual way.<ref name=":0" />

;'''VC'''
: Lewis's "official" logic of counterfactuals '''VC''' adds (CS) to VW.  VC is thus the smallest normal logic extending V that validates both (SM) and (CS); in Lewis's sphere semantics this corresponds to total preorders with additional constraints ensuring that whenever both <math>A</math> and <math>A\land B</math> are possible, <math>A \land B</math>–worlds are among the closest <math>A</math>–worlds.<ref name="Lewis1973" /><ref name=":0" />

;'''C2'''
: Stalnaker's logic '''C2''' can be obtained from VC by replacing (CS) with the stronger (CEM).  C2 is thus VC + (CEM), and it characterizes the simplified Stalnaker models in which each antecedent selects a unique closest antecedent world at every evaluation point.<ref name="Stalnaker1968" /><ref name="StalnakerThomason1970"/><ref name=":0" />

;'''SS'''
: Pollock's system '''SS''' is obtained by adding (SM) and (CS) directly to B (rather than via V).  It validates many of the same laws as VC but is based on partial, rather than total, similarity orderings.<ref name="Pollock1976">{{cite book |last=Pollock |first=John L. |year=1976 |title=Subjunctive Reasoning |publisher=Reidel}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

;'''NP'''
: Delgrande's system '''NP''' is another extension of CK: like B it validates (ID), (AND), (OR) and (CCut), but instead of (CMon) it validates (RMon).  This shows that the cautious and rational forms of monotonicity are independent over CK.<ref name="Delgrande1987">{{cite journal |last=Delgrande |first=James |year=1987 |title=A First-Order Conditional Logic for Prototypical Properties |journal=Artificial Intelligence |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=105–130 |doi=10.1016/0004-3702(87)90023-6}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

These systems all validate (LT) and (AND), differ on the status of (ID), (OR), (CCut), (CMon), (Rec), (RMon), (SM), (CS) and (CEM), and none validates full Monotonicity, Transitivity or Contraposition for <math>\mathbin{>}</math>.<ref name=":0" />

=== Selection function axiomatizations (Lewis–Nute tradition) ===

An alternative but equivalent presentation of many of the above systems is widely used in the Lewis–Nute tradition, and is convenient when relating conditional logics directly to selection function semantics.<ref name="Nute1980" /><ref>{{Citation|title=Conditional Logic|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-6259-0_8|publisher=Springer Netherlands|work=Handbook of Philosophical Logic: Volume II: Extensions of Classical Logic|date=1984|first=Donald|last=Nute}}</ref>  In this type of axiomatization, one takes as primitive:

* all propositional tautologies in the language with <math>\mathbin{>}</math>;
* the rule (MP);
* one or both of the "replacement" rules

::'''(RCEC)''' from <math>\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi</math>, infer <math>(\chi \mathbin{>} \varphi) \leftrightarrow (\chi \mathbin{>} \psi)</math>;
::'''(RCEA)''' from <math>\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi</math>, infer <math>(\varphi \mathbin{>} \chi) \leftrightarrow (\psi \mathbin{>} \chi)</math>;

* and the rule

::'''(RCK)''' as above.

In this setting, the Lewis systems V, VW, VC and Stalnaker's C2 can be described as the smallest conditional logics containing all tautologies, closed under (MP), (RCEC) and (RCK), and containing all substitution instances of appropriate sets of schemata such as:

:'''ID''' <math>\varphi \mathbin{>} \varphi</math>;
:'''MP/SM''' <math>(\varphi \mathbin{>} \psi) \to (\varphi \to \psi)</math>;
:'''MOD''' <math>(\neg \varphi \mathbin{>} \varphi) \to (\psi \mathbin{>} \varphi)</math>;
:'''CSO''' <math>((\varphi \mathbin{>} \psi)\land(\psi \mathbin{>} \varphi)) \to ((\varphi \mathbin{>} \chi) \leftrightarrow (\psi \mathbin{>} \chi))</math>;
:'''CV''' <math>((\varphi \mathbin{>} \psi)\land\neg(\varphi \mathbin{>} \neg \chi)) \to ((\varphi \land \chi) \mathbin{>} \psi)</math>;
:'''CS''' <math>(\varphi \land \psi) \to (\varphi \mathbin{>} \psi)</math>;
:'''CEM''' <math>(\varphi \mathbin{>} \psi) \lor (\varphi \mathbin{>} \neg \psi)</math>.

For example, one standard presentation takes:<ref name="Nute1980" /><ref name=":0" />

* '''V''' as the smallest logic with (RCEC), (RCK) and schemata ID, MOD, CSO, CV;
* '''VW''' as V + (SM);
* '''VC''' as VW + (CS);
* '''C2''' as VC with (CS) replaced by (CEM).

These axiomatizations are equivalent to the ones described via the Table 6 schemata above and are often used in proof theory and automated reasoning for conditional logics.<ref name="Olivetti 2007 22"/>

=== Nonmonotonic consequence systems C, P and R ===

In artificial intelligence and nonmonotonic reasoning it is common to work, not directly with a connective <math>\mathbin{>}</math>, but with a defeasible consequence relation <math>\vdash_{\!\sim}</math> intended to capture defaults of the form "normally, if <math>A</math> then <math>B</math>".  Kraus, Lehmann and Magidor axiomatized three central such systems, now known as C, P and R.<ref name="KLM1990">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Kraus
 | first1 = Sarit
 | last2 = Lehmann
 | first2 = Daniel
 | last3 = Magidor
 | first3 = Menachem
 | year = 1990
 | title = Nonmonotonic Reasoning, Preferential Models and Cumulative Logics
 | journal = Artificial Intelligence
 | volume = 44
 | issue = 1–2
 | pages = 167–207
 | doi = 10.1016/0004-3702(90)90101-5
}}</ref>
<ref name=":0" />

These systems are given by rules on <math>\vdash_{\!\sim}</math> such as:

:* '''(ID<sub>~</sub>)''' Identity: <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} A</math>.
:* '''(LLE<sub>~</sub>)''' Left logical equivalence: if <math>\vDash A \equiv B</math> and <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>, then <math>B \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>.
:* '''(RW<sub>~</sub>)''' Right weakening: if <math>\vDash C \to D</math> and <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>, then <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} D</math>.
:* '''(CCut<sub>~</sub>)''' Cautious cut: from <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} B</math> and <math>A \land B \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>, infer <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>.
:* '''(CMon<sub>~</sub>)''' Cautious monotonicity: from <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} B</math> and <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>, infer <math>A \land B \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>.
:* '''(AND<sub>~</sub>)''' And: from <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} B</math> and <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>, infer <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} (B \land C)</math>.
:* '''(OR<sub>~</sub>)''' Or: from <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math> and <math>B \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>, infer <math>A \lor B \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>.
:* '''(RMon<sub>~</sub>)''' Rational monotonicity: from <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math> and not <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} \neg B</math>, infer <math>A \land B \vdash_{\!\sim} C</math>.

On this basis one defines:

* System '''C''' (cumulative): the smallest relation satisfying (ID<sub>~</sub>), (LLE<sub>~</sub>), (RW<sub>~</sub>), (CCut<sub>~</sub>) and (CMon<sub>~</sub>) (and hence (AND<sub>~</sub>)).
* System '''P''' (preferential): C plus (OR<sub>~</sub>); it is sound and complete for preferential models and corresponds to the "flat" (<math>L_1</math>) fragment of several conditional logics such as B and VC.<ref name="KLM1990" /><ref name=":0" />
* System '''R''' (rational): P plus (RMon<sub>~</sub>); it is complete for ranked (totally ordered) preferential models.

Via translations of the form "<math>A \mathbin{>} B</math> is accepted iff <math>A \vdash_{\!\sim} B</math>", these nonmonotonic systems can be seen as providing the flat fragments of many of the selection–function conditional logics described above, linking conditional logic to AGM belief revision and default reasoning.<ref name="KLM1990" /><ref name="Gärdenfors1988">{{cite book |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1988 |title=Knowledge in Flux |publisher=MIT Press}}</ref>
